_how: The crew as data. One entry per division, one per worker. Adding a worker is adding an entry here: 'impl' names its implementation in workers.IMPLS, 'provider' names an entry in 'providers' (the minimum seconds between two requests to that host, shared by every worker on it), 'uses' lists the Pionir capabilities its code calls (reported by /api/divisions; tests/test_crew_uses.py holds it to the code). Worker ids are '<division>.<name>' and must be unique; an unknown field, impl, provider or division is an error at load time. Moss is not in this file: she is a separate process (C:\src\Galatea) that reads the leaders' reports and sets each division's goal and compute share.

workers.name: ledger
workers.note: Scrooge's ledger, read-only

workers.name: fiverr
workers.note: the Fiverr-reported gross (from Fiverr's order emails, via the Fiverr desk's record); not our revenue records

divisions.leader_notes: treasury.ledger is Scrooge's ledger: our revenue. treasury.fiverr is different: fiverr.earnings holds the Fiverr-reported gross - the prices Fiverr's order emails state, before Fiverr's fee - for orders not cancelled and for completed orders. Always call it Fiverr-reported gross, report it separately, and never add it to our revenue or call it revenue: Fiverr keeps its fee and pays out on its own schedule, and Scrooge's ledger never sees it. Orders whose price was not a plain US dollar amount are counted, never valued. When treasury.fiverr has not run or cannot read the desk's record, Fiverr earnings are UNKNOWN, never zero. treasury.bolts is a play-currency tally: Bolts are never revenue and never money, so never add them to any figure above or call them earnings; report them as Bolts only. When a source it reads is UNKNOWN, say UNKNOWN, never zero.

workers.name: health
workers.note: is api.dokaz.net up

divisions.title: Posting
divisions.leader_notes: Four workers post: posting.blog (blog posts on the website), posting.instagram (Instagram card posts), posting.devto (each published blog post cross-posted to dev.to, unchanged) and posting.newsletter (once a week, an email to the newsletter's confirmed subscribers listing the week's published posts, the tools on sale and the hire page; assembled, not written). Each row names its worker; report them separately. posting.newsletter's newsletter.audience row is the list as the site counts it: subscribers confirmed, waiting to confirm and unsubscribed, newsletters sent, and the last send's recipients, emails sent and failed; newsletter.audience_unavailable says why the list could not be read, and then its counts are UNKNOWN, never zero. Its post.tally payload this_week says whether this week's newsletter was submitted, or skipped because nothing was new or because the list has no confirmed subscriber yet, or because Scrooge cannot send newsletters yet (the worker is then NOT CONFIGURED: the site's postal address or mail key is not set; say exactly that). A post.not_published row with status not_configured is a newsletter the owner approved that Scrooge could not send for that reason: it did NOT go out. A newsletter PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been sent. Each worker's post.tally holds its counts: drafts written, drafts blocked, posts submitted for approval, posts pending approval, posts published, posts denied (for posting.devto: cross-posts, and published blog posts waiting to be cross-posted). A post PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been published: say it is waiting for the owner's approval, never that it is out. Only a post.published row is a published post; give its URL for the blog and dev.to, its permalink for Instagram. A post.blocked row is a draft the content check stopped before anyone saw it: say so and give its reasons by kind (a name not on the allowlist, a link or domain, personal data, a business number, an internal system name, text that does not fit the Instagram card) without repeating any name the reasons quote. A post.not_published row says why a submitted post did not go out (denied by the owner, failed, or done without a URL or permalink). posting.results reads the site's own visit counter for the last 30 days: traffic.working is the plain summary (read it first), traffic.site the site and each channel (blog links, instagram bio, dev.to, search), traffic.posts each published post by its slug (page views, clicks to product pages, dev.to visits, sales), traffic.sales sales and net revenue per campaign, traffic.instagram each published Instagram post by its draft id (lifetime reach, likes, comments, saves, shares, interactions and views, from Instagram's own insights, measured at the time it gives). An Instagram metric listed as unavailable has no number: never write it as zero. When traffic.instagram says there are no Instagram insights yet, or that they are unavailable, say exactly that. Use these figures to suggest which topics to do more of, naming each post by its slug with its figures as recorded. Say what the numbers show, never why: one post doing well is not proof that its topic caused it, so never claim cause from one data point. A post with fewer than 20 page views is too early to tell: say so, and draw nothing from it. A figure marked 'at least' is a lower bound, and a post listed as unknown has no number: never write it as zero. When traffic.working says there is no traffic data yet, say exactly that and suggest nothing about topics.

workers.name: blog
workers.note: one checked blog draft a day for api.dokaz.net, each submitted for the owner's approval; topics from what we sell by measured demand; a blocked draft is mended and redrafted within a daily budget; after 3 blocked drafts in a day, at most one claude -p draft (Max, sonnet-class), checked and approved like any other

workers.name: instagram
workers.note: one checked Instagram card post a day, each submitted for the owner's approval

workers.name: devto
workers.note: each published blog post cross-posted to dev.to once, checked, for the owner's approval

workers.name: newsletter
workers.note: once a week, the newsletter assembled from the week's published posts and the tools on sale, checked, for the owner's approval; the subscriber counts from the site; no model

workers.name: results
workers.note: what the posts did: the site's page views, clicks and sales by post and channel, last 30 days; each Instagram post's own insights

divisions.title: Contracts
divisions.leader_notes: Four workers: contracts.orders, the order desk, contracts.delivery, the delivery desk, contracts.finder, the finder, and contracts.feedback, the feedback desk; each row names its worker, report them separately. The order desk reads the client orders for paid 'I do it for you' work and answers each by a fixed template (an acknowledgement, a quote acknowledgement or a decline), each parked for the owner's approval before it is sent. Report NEW PAID ORDERS first and prominently: they are money. Each order.new_paid row is one, with its order id, package and amount as recorded. order.tally holds the counts: orders by status, paid orders waiting for acknowledgement, paid orders held for the owner, acknowledgements sent, quote acknowledgements sent, quote requests waiting for the owner, flagged orders awaiting the owner, declines sent, refunds to issue by hand in Stripe, abandoned checkouts, paid revenue in the orders listed, and client emails pending the owner's approval, denied, failed and blocked. The desk also offers ONE checkout-recovery email (email kind recovery) to an order whose Stripe checkout expired unpaid: a fixed template with the order's package and Stripe's recovery link, parked for the owner's approval, never offered again once sent or denied, and never to an order that paid. order.tally counts checkouts expired, recovery emails pending the owner's approval, recovery emails approved and sent, recovery emails denied, orders recovered (paid after their recovery email) and recovered revenue: a recovery email PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been sent, and only an order that paid after its recovery email went is recovered. An email PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been sent: say it is waiting for the owner. Only an order.email_sent row is a sent email. Never promise a client anything, and never state a price, a date, a turnaround or a delivery beyond what the rows record: the desk sends only its fixed templates. Flagged orders (the brief matched a category the owner declines, named in the row's flags) and quote requests need the owner: say so with their order ids, and say that a flag is only a flag until the owner approves the decline. Paid orders held for the owner (a package or amount the templates do not cover) need him too. Refunds are never automated: a declined paid order is a refund the owner issues by hand in Stripe, so say how many are waiting. When the orders could not be read, say they are UNKNOWN, never zero. contracts.delivery ships each order's finished work: the owner drops a zip in the order's folder, and the desk submits it as a delivery email with a private download link, parked for the owner's approval. delivery.tally holds the counts: orders in progress, orders in progress with no delivery yet (waiting for a zip), orders past their turnaround, deliveries pending the owner's approval, deliveries delivered, revised deliveries delivered, deliveries blocked by the checks, deliveries denied, failed, and approved deliveries that failed to send (offered to the owner again). A delivery PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been delivered, and nothing is delivered until a delivery.delivered row says so: never say or imply a client has their work before that row. A delivery.blocked row is URGENT for the owner: Pionir's checks refused the zip before anyone saw it (for example a secret found in it, an executable, or no README or HOWTO); give the order id and the reason, and say the client is still waiting until he drops a fixed zip - the same zip is never tried again. The tally's blocked list holds each blocked order's reason. Orders past their turnaround are late: say so with their order ids. When the orders could not be read, the deliveries are UNKNOWN, never 'nothing to deliver'. contracts.finder handles 'Find it for me' orders ($19 flat, a report of where to buy something within 2 business days, a full refund if nothing is found): once the order desk's acknowledgement is sent, it asks Claude to research the item on the web (counted against the daily Claude cap), checks the answer, and submits the client's report, parked for the owner's approval. find.tally holds the counts: find orders in progress, find orders waiting for research, find orders waiting for Claude budget, research runs, research failures, find reports pending the owner's approval, find reports sent, not-found reports sent, refunds to issue by hand in Stripe, find reports blocked, denied and failed, affiliate programs set up, find reports sent with affiliate links and affiliate links in find reports sent (reports and links that carried the owner's affiliate tag, disclosed to the client). Affiliate COMMISSIONS are not observed: they show only in each program's own reporting, so never state or estimate affiliate revenue. A find.research_failed row is URGENT for the owner: Claude's research was missing or failed the checks twice (or the brief must not be researched), nothing was sent, and the client is waiting - give the order id and the reasons. A find.report_blocked row is URGENT too: the report was refused before anyone saw it; give the order id and the reason, and say it is never resent. Orders waiting for Claude budget are waiting, not skipped: say so. A report PENDING APPROVAL has NOT been sent; only a find.report_sent row is a sent report. A not-found report sent is a refund the owner issues by hand in Stripe: say how many are waiting. Never promise a client a price, a stock level or a find: prices and stock are the sellers', they change, and only the report states them. contracts.feedback asks each delivered client, once and never sooner than 3 days after delivery, how it went (a fixed template with a private feedback link and their referral code, parked for the owner's approval like every client email), and proposes each testimonial a client consented to show for the owner's approval before it appears on the hire page. feedback.tally holds the counts: delivered orders due a feedback request, feedback requests pending the owner's approval, sent, denied, failed and blocked, testimonials pending the owner's approval, blocked by the content checks and declined, and from Scrooge: feedback requests sent, feedback answers received, the average client rating in stars out of 5, testimonials live on the hire page, orders placed through a referral code, referral orders paid, and referral credits to apply by hand. A request or testimonial PENDING APPROVAL has not been sent or shown. A feedback.testimonial_blocked row means a client's words failed the content checks and were never proposed: say so with its id. Referral credits ($25 off the referrer's next order) are records the owner applies by hand: never say a discount or refund was given. Never quote a client's words or name: the rows carry ids and counts only.

workers.name: orders
workers.note: every client order answered by fixed template (acknowledgement, quote acknowledgement or decline), each email for the owner's approval; no model

workers.name: delivery
workers.note: each order's finished zip (dropped by the owner in its order's folder) delivered to its client by fixed template, for the owner's approval; no model

workers.name: finder
workers.note: each paid 'Find it for me' order researched by Claude with web tools only (daily Claude cap), checked, and reported to its client by fixed template, for the owner's approval

workers.name: feedback
workers.note: one feedback request per delivered order (fixed template, 3+ days after delivery) and each consented testimonial proposed for /hire, every one for the owner's approval; no model

divisions.title: Products
divisions.leader_notes: products.shelf puts the products the owner stages on sale on Gumroad, each only after the owner approves it on Discord, and reads what the live ones sold. Report NEW SALES first and prominently: they are money. Each product.new_sales row is one product whose sales count rose since the last look, with its slug, the new sales and its totals as Gumroad reports them. A product.blocked row is URGENT for the owner: Pionir's checks refused the product before anyone saw it (for example a secret found in the zip, no README, an executable, a cover too small); give its slug, version and the reason, and say it stays off sale until he stages fixed files - the same content is never tried again. The tally's blocked list holds each blocked product's reason. A product.listing_malformed row, and the tally's malformed list, is a listing.json that failed the shelf's own check and was NOT submitted: give the folder and the reasons. Never call a product live, on sale or published until a product.published row says so (or product.sales lists it as live): a product PENDING APPROVAL is waiting for the owner and is NOT on sale. A product.not_published row says why a submitted product did not go out (denied by the owner, failed, or an approved one that failed to publish and will be offered to him again). product.tally holds the counts: products staged, staged but not yet approved, pending the owner's approval, blocked by the checks, denied by the owner, malformed listings, failed, and product versions published. product.sales holds each live product's sales and revenue as Gumroad reports them (stream = the product's slug), and the totals (stream all). When the newest row is product.sales_unavailable, the sales and revenue are UNKNOWN, never zero: say so. Suggest a price or listing change only from the sales recorded in product.sales, naming the product by its slug with its figures as recorded; never invent a sale, a price or a trend, and never claim why a product sold. products.api_builder writes one paid API product at a time for the Dokaz API: it takes the next idea from the owner's backlog (seed ideas are UNVALIDATED guesses, say so), has Daedalus (a local model) write it overnight in a scaffold repo, checks it contained, has Claude review it once (and edit it once if the review finds a small fixable problem), and stages it on a local branch for the owner. Nothing is ever deployed, published or paid for by it. An api.pending row is a staged product waiting for the owner's yes to run its checks: it is NOT built, NOT verified and NOT live. An api.verified row means tsc and the tests passed on that branch after he approved them, and the branch is ready for him to review and deploy himself; it is still NOT live. An api.red row means a check failed: give the id and which check, never say it works. An api.shelved row is a product whose builds never passed the checks (the owner raises retry on its backlog entry to try again); an api.denied row is one the owner did not approve; an api.failed row could not be staged or checked, with its reason. An api.waiting row means the build waits (the overnight window is closed, Daedalus or the GPU is busy, or Claude's per-night or daily cap or usage window is spent): not a fault. An api.started row is a Daedalus build begun overnight; api.built means Daedalus finished and our checks and Claude's review are next; api.attempt_failed and api.rejected mean a build failed our checks or its own gate and goes back to Daedalus once; api.review_failed means Claude's review or edit could not be completed and is retried; an api.staged row says whether Claude edited it. An api.backlog_invalid row lists backlog entries that failed the checks and were not built. An api.not_set_up row means Pionir lacks the apibuild.verify capability. A worker error saying NOT SET UP means the sandbox user or its node was not set up (the owner re-runs tools\setup-build-sandbox.ps1 elevated); nothing is built until then. api.tally holds the counts: queued, in progress, waiting on the owner, verified, red, shelved, denied, failed, invalid, and any product that needs its old branch removed before a retry. Never invent an endpoint, a price, a customer or a sale for an API product. With no sales recorded yet, say exactly that and suggest nothing about prices. products.demand ranks what to build and sell next from MEASURED demand only (the dash's API usage over 14 days and its traffic over 30 days) and writes it to demand.json, which steers the Builds backlog pick and the blog's topic choice when Moss's goal names none. Its demand.ranking row lists the top candidates (an api, a free tool, a blog topic, a Builds backlog product or an API builder idea) with each one's demand score and the inputs it came from; report the top three exactly as recorded, each with its inputs. A demand score is a weighted sum that only orders candidates: never call it money, sales, visitors or a forecast. A partial score had an input that could not be measured and is a lower bound; a candidate listed as unknown has NO score: never write it as zero. The signals in its unavailable list (per-tool click-throughs, rejected 429 calls, free versus paid calls, calls per endpoint, search referrals per post) are not recorded anywhere: say they are UNKNOWN if asked, never estimate them. A demand.card row is a suggestion card posted to the owner (demand seen: X - suggest Y): it added nothing to any backlog and built nothing; demand.card_unposted says why one did not reach him. Never claim why demand is high.

workers.name: shelf
workers.note: each product staged in its own folder published on Gumroad, for the owner's approval, and the live products' sales as Gumroad reports them; no model

workers.name: demand
workers.note: what to build and sell next, ranked daily from measured demand only (API usage and traffic from the dash; UNKNOWN never zero), written to demand.json for the Builds pick and the blog's topics; at most one suggestion card a day, never an edit to a backlog; no model

workers.name: api_builder
workers.note: one paid API product a night written by Daedalus (local, free) in a fresh scaffold repo inside the overnight GPU window, checked contained, then ONE Claude review and at most one Claude edit (cheaper model, per-night cap) before it is staged on a local branch of the Scrooge repo; its real tsc and test run happens only on the owner's approval; never deploys

divisions.title: Fiverr
divisions.leader_notes: Three workers: fiverr.ideas hands the owner ONE new gig idea at a time, chosen from our own measured product demand (fiverr.idea_proposed) - say that demand is measured on our own sites and is NOT Fiverr search volume, that nothing is posted to Fiverr, and that Pionir has no automatic delivery for an idea gig yet (an order for it stops for the owner). fiverr.idea_decided is his skip or listed reply; fiverr.idea_blocked means the idea failed its checks and nothing was sent; fiverr.idea_tally holds the counts. fiverr.gigs drafts one listing per service (research, data, website, uptime) for the owner to paste into Fiverr himself, and fiverr.desk prepares each Fiverr order for him to deliver. Nothing in the crew or Pionir logs into, posts to or messages on Fiverr: the owner does every Fiverr step himself. A READY card (fiverr.ready, fiverr.order_ready) means the files and a drafted reply are waiting for the OWNER to upload and send on Fiverr - never say the buyer has anything, or that anything was delivered or sent, until fiverr.order_delivered says Fiverr marked the order completed. Report NEW ORDERS (fiverr.order_new) first, with their order numbers and service. A fiverr.problem row is URGENT: nothing was prepared for that order (a check failed, the research or the website failed twice, or the brief names no site) - give the order number and the reasons; the order waits for the owner. Orders waiting for the buyer's files or for Claude's budget are waiting, not failed. fiverr.tally holds the counts: orders by state (new, brief received, working, ready, delivered, cancelled), orders stopped for the owner, orders waiting, READY cards posted, revisions asked, buyer messages with a drafted reply, events applied, unknown events, events not yet acknowledged, the median time from brief to ready, and the Fiverr-reported gross. The gross is what Fiverr's emails state, before Fiverr's fee: always call it Fiverr-reported gross, never revenue or earnings of ours. fiverr.gig_tally holds the gigs drafted, blocked, and the packages waiting for the owner's price: a package with no price is waiting for HIM - the crew only proposes, and never state a proposed price as a gig's price. A fiverr.cards_unposted row means cards for the owner have not reached Discord for over an hour (they are retried every run): say so plainly. When the desk could not read the events, the orders are UNKNOWN, never zero.

workers.name: gigs
workers.note: one checked Fiverr listing per service, handed to the owner on Discord to paste into Fiverr himself; redrafted only when he replies redraft or sets prices

workers.name: ideas
workers.note: one new Fiverr gig idea at a time, picked from measured product demand and handed to the owner on Discord; he accepts, skips or sets prices, and creates the gig on Fiverr himself

workers.name: desk
workers.note: each Fiverr order from Scrooge's events to a READY card (files and a drafted reply) that the owner delivers on Fiverr himself; research and websites by Claude on the daily cap

divisions.title: Builds
divisions.leader_notes: builds.daedalus builds the owner's small paid developer tools ($9-19 each on Gumroad), back to back while the night's window has room: a contained Daedalus (a separate, firewalled Windows user) writes it in its own fresh sandbox repo, ONLY inside the overnight window (build.tally's window, local time) because it takes the whole GPU, one job at a time; then our own checks (the product's tests run by us, no network access, no secrets or owner data, the licence) and Claude's review. Only a build Claude APPROVED is staged on the product shelf, and a staged product is NOT on sale: products.shelf submits it for the owner's approval like every product, so never call a built or staged product live, published or on sale. Report each build.staged row first (the product's slug, name and listing price as recorded), then each build.shelved row with its reason (a build rejected again after its one repair, one whose review could not be completed, or one that could not be staged). A build.rejected row is a review that said no, with its reasons: its one repair follows. build.attempt_failed is a Daedalus attempt that failed its own gate or ran out of time: a repair follows. A build.second_life row is a shelved product getting its ONE more attempt (kind timeout, nothing_committed or tests_failed); it is not built or staged until a later build.staged row says so. A build.shelved row with second_life false is final, and its terminal_why says why. build.waiting means Daedalus, the GPU or Claude's budget was not available: the build waits, it did not fail. When the worker reports NOT CONFIGURED, the owner has not yet run tools\setup-build-sandbox.ps1: nothing is built until he does - say exactly that. build.tally holds the counts: products staged, shelved, in progress (with what each waits for), the backlog's next products, whether Daedalus is down, and cards that did not reach Discord. The owner edits the backlog by replying to the Builds cards; build.backlog_reply rows say what his replies changed. Never invent a sale, a price or a product; prices are the listing prices the rows state, never revenue.

workers.name: daedalus
workers.note: small developer tools built back to back through the night (each shelved one gets one second life if it timed out, committed nothing or failed its tests), built by Daedalus in a fresh sandbox repo inside the overnight GPU window, reviewed by Claude on the daily cap, and staged for the product shelf (still the owner's approval before any sale)
